paras.en: The oldest paradoxes we have come from Zeno of Elea, a Greek of the fifth century BCE. His teacher Parmenides had argued that reality is one and unchanging and that motion is an appearance. Zeno defended him by showing that the commonsense view, on which things move, leads to absurdities of its own. Aristotle preserves the most famous of his arguments: “in a race the quickest runner can never overtake the slowest, since the pursuer must first reach the point whence the pursued started, so that the slower must always hold a lead.”
paras.zh: 我們手上最古老的悖論出自埃利亞的芝諾，西元前五世紀的希臘人。他的老師巴門尼德主張，實在是唯一而不變的，運動只是表象。芝諾替老師辯護的方式，是證明常識的看法——東西會動——自己會導出荒謬。亞里斯多德保存了他最有名的一個論證：「在賽跑中，跑得最快的永遠追不上最慢的，因為追的人必須先到達被追的人出發的那一點，所以慢的那個必定一直保持領先。」

paras.en: Give the slow runner a start of a hundred meters. By the time Achilles has covered the hundred, the other has crept forward ten. By the time Achilles has covered those ten, it is one meter further on, and so without end. At every stage a gap remains. The stages never run out. So it seems that Achilles is always on the point of drawing level and never does.
paras.zh: 讓慢的那個先跑一百公尺。等阿基里斯跑完這一百公尺，對方已經往前爬了十公尺。等阿基里斯跑完這十公尺，牠又在前面一公尺了；如此下去，沒有盡頭。每一個階段都還剩一段差距，而階段永遠用不完。於是看起來，阿基里斯永遠就要追平，卻永遠沒有追平。

paras.en: Chinese thinkers found the same puzzle independently. The last chapter of the Zhuangzi records a saying of the debaters around Hui Shi, in the fourth century BCE: “A stick one foot long: take away half of it every day, and in ten thousand generations it will not be used up.” This is Zeno’s other great argument, the Dichotomy, turned from motion to matter. Before you reach the door you must reach the halfway point, and before that the halfway point of the first half. Run in one direction the argument says you never arrive, and run in the other it says you can never set out.
paras.zh: 中國的思想家各自獨立地發現了同一個難題。《莊子》最後一篇記下了西元前四世紀惠施周圍那群辯者的一句話：「一尺之捶，日取其半，萬世不竭。」這是芝諾另一個重要論證「二分法」，只是從運動換成了物質。你走到門口之前，必須先走到一半；在那之前，又必須先走到前一半的一半。這個論證往一個方向推，說你永遠到不了；往另一個方向推，說你根本出發不了。

essay.h_en: The sum of infinitely many things

paras.en: The standard answer took two thousand years to state properly. Zeno assumes that infinitely many distances, or infinitely many intervals of time, must add up to an infinite amount. They need not. The distances in the race are 100, 10, 1, 0.1 and so on, and the more of them you add, the closer the total comes to 111.11… meters without ever exceeding it. Mathematicians of the nineteenth century, Cauchy foremost among them, made this exact with the concept of a limit. The times behave the same way. If Achilles runs ten meters a second, the stages take 10 seconds, then 1, then 0.1, and all of them together take 11.11… seconds. After that he is in front.
paras.zh: 標準答案花了兩千年才被說清楚。芝諾假定，無窮多段距離，或無窮多段時間，加起來一定是無窮大。其實不必。賽跑裡的各段距離是 100、10、1、0.1……，你加進去的項愈多，總和就愈接近 111.11… 公尺，卻永遠不會超過它。十九世紀的數學家，以柯西為首，用「極限」這個概念把這件事說得精確。時間也是同樣的情形。如果阿基里斯每秒跑十公尺，各階段分別花 10 秒、1 秒、0.1 秒……，全部加起來是 11.11… 秒。在那之後，他就在前面了。

paras.en: Many philosophers think this dissolves the paradox, and many do not. The arithmetic tells us where and when Achilles draws level. It does not obviously tell us how anyone finishes a sequence of tasks that has no last member. In 1954 James Thomson sharpened the worry with a lamp. Switch it on for a minute, off for half a minute, on for a quarter, and so on; after two minutes infinitely many switchings are done. Is the lamp then on or off? It cannot be on, since every time it was turned on it was turned off again, and it cannot be off for the same reason. Thomson concluded that completing infinitely many tasks, a “supertask,” is impossible. His critics replied that the story merely fails to say what happens at two minutes. The argument continues, and what is at stake in it is whether space, time, and motion are really as the mathematics of the continuum describes them.
paras.zh: 許多哲學家認為這樣就化解了悖論，也有許多人不這麼想。算術告訴我們阿基里斯在哪裡、在什麼時候追平。可是，一個沒有「最後一項」的任務序列，到底是怎麼被做完的，算術並沒有明白地告訴我們。1954 年，湯姆森用一盞燈把這個疑慮磨得更尖。把燈打開一分鐘，關掉半分鐘，再開四分之一分鐘，如此下去；兩分鐘後，無窮多次開關都做完了。這時燈是亮的還是暗的？它不可能是亮的，因為每一次打開之後都又被關掉了；基於同樣的理由，它也不可能是暗的。湯姆森的結論是：完成無窮多個任務，也就是所謂的「超任務」，是不可能的。批評他的人回答說，這個故事只是沒有交代兩分鐘那一刻發生了什麼。這場爭論還在繼續；而它真正牽涉到的是：空間、時間與運動，是不是真的像連續統的數學所描述的那樣。

essay.h_en: A sentence that turns on itself
essay.h_zh: 一個回頭咬自己的句子

paras.en: A second family of paradoxes needs no racetrack, only a sentence. Consider: “This sentence is false.” If it is true, then what it says is the case, so it is false. If it is false, then what it says is not the case, so it is true. The ancient version is credited to Eubulides, a contemporary of Aristotle, and it is known as the Liar. It is tempting to dismiss the Liar as a trick, and for two thousand years most people did. Then, in the early twentieth century, the same structure of self-reference turned up in the foundations of mathematics. Bertrand Russell found it in the notion of a set, and Kurt Gödel used a relative of the Liar, a sentence that says of itself that it cannot be proved, to show that arithmetic contains truths no consistent system of rules can derive. Alfred Tarski’s response to the Liar was that no language can contain its own truth predicate: to say of a sentence that it is true, one has to step up into a richer language. Ordinary English falls short of that standard, which may mean that ordinary English is, strictly speaking, inconsistent.
paras.zh: 第二個家族的悖論不需要跑道，只需要一個句子。請看：「這個句子是假的。」如果它是真的，那麼它說的就是事實，所以它是假的。如果它是假的，那麼它說的就不是事實，所以它是真的。它的古代版本相傳出自與亞里斯多德同時代的歐布利德斯，稱為「說謊者悖論」。把說謊者當成文字把戲打發掉，是很誘人的做法；兩千年來，多數人正是這樣做的。然後在二十世紀初，同一種自我指涉的結構，出現在數學的基礎裡。羅素在「集合」這個概念裡發現了它；哥德爾則用了說謊者的一個親戚——一個說自己「不可被證明」的句子——證明算術裡有些真理，是任何一致的規則系統都推導不出來的。塔斯基對說謊者的回應是：沒有任何語言能包含它自己的「真」這個謂詞；要說一個句子是真的，就得往上跨進一個更豐富的語言。日常的英語達不到這個標準；這也許表示，嚴格說來，日常的英語是不一致的。

paras.en: Eubulides is also credited with the paradox of the heap, the sorites. One grain of sand is not a heap. Adding a single grain to something that is not a heap never turns it into one. So no number of grains makes a heap. Each premise seems undeniable, the logic is modus ponens repeated, and the conclusion is false. What makes the sorites so hard is that the trouble is everywhere. “Heap” is vague, and so are “tall,” “adult,” “alive,” and “person,” and the same argument can be run on each of them. Law and ethics depend on such words, and on lines that have to be drawn somewhere although no particular place for them can be defended.
paras.zh: 相傳「堆垛悖論」（sorites）也出自歐布利德斯。一粒沙不是一堆。在不成堆的東西上加一粒沙，絕不會讓它變成一堆。所以不管多少粒沙，都不成一堆。每一個前提看來都無法否認，邏輯只是反覆使用肯定前件，而結論是假的。堆垛悖論之所以這麼難，是因為問題無所不在。「堆」是模糊的，「高」「成年」「活著」「人」也都是；同一個論證可以套在每一個詞上。法律與倫理都仰賴這類詞語，也仰賴那些總得畫在某處的界線；儘管沒有哪一個特定的位置能被辯護。

paras.en: It would be a mistake to file all this under puzzles. A paradox is an argument that our own concepts make against us. It shows that what we believe about motion, or truth, or the meaning of ordinary words cannot all be right together, and it does so using nothing except those beliefs. The great ones are therefore never simply solved. They are answered by changing something: by inventing the limit, or separating a language from its metalanguage, or by rethinking what a set is. With this the first unit ends, on a caution. Logic can show us that our premises conflict. It does not tell us which of them to give up.
paras.zh: 把這一切歸到「益智謎題」那一類，會是個錯誤。悖論是我們自己的概念對我們提出的論證。它證明我們對運動、對真、對日常詞語意義的種種信念，不可能同時全部正確；而且它除了這些信念之外，什麼都沒用到。所以偉大的悖論從來不是單純被「解開」的。回應它們的方式，是改變某樣東西：發明極限，或把一個語言跟它的後設語言分開，或重新思考集合是什麼。第一個單元就在這裡結束，結束在一句提醒上：邏輯能告訴我們，我們的前提互相衝突；它不告訴我們該放棄哪一個。

lab.title_en: Try it: run the race two ways
lab.title_zh: 親手做一次：用兩種方式跑這場比賽
lab.lead_en: First run the race Zeno’s way, one stage at a time, and watch the gap shrink without ever closing. Then let the clock run and watch Achilles go past. The same race is being described both times, and the paradox is the question of how both descriptions can be right.
lab.lead_zh: 先照芝諾的方式跑，一次一個階段，看差距不斷縮小卻始終沒有合上。然後讓時鐘自己走，看阿基里斯超過去。兩次描述的是同一場比賽；悖論就是在問：這兩種描述怎麼可能都對？
lab.note_en: Achilles runs 10 meters a second. The tortoise starts 100 meters ahead.
lab.note_zh: 阿基里斯每秒跑 10 公尺。烏龜從前方 100 公尺處出發。

argument.lead_en: Set out step by step, the Achilles has four premises. Anyone who rejects the conclusion owes Zeno an answer to the question of which one is false. Click a step to see what can be said against it.
argument.lead_zh: 一步一步攤開來，阿基里斯論證有四個前提。任何不接受結論的人，都欠芝諾一個答案：哪一個前提是假的？點任何一步，看看別人可以怎麼反對它。

steps.en: To catch the tortoise, Achilles must first reach the point where the tortoise was when he set out.
steps.zh: 要追上烏龜，阿基里斯必須先到達他出發時烏龜所在的那一點。
steps.ob_en: Hardly deniable, given that he runs along the same line. This premise only describes the race.
steps.ob_zh: 既然他沿著同一條線跑，這幾乎無法否認。這個前提只是在描述比賽。

steps.en: Whenever Achilles reaches a point where the tortoise was, the tortoise has moved some distance ahead.
steps.zh: 每當阿基里斯到達烏龜曾經在的某一點，烏龜已經往前移動了一段距離。
steps.ob_en: True for as long as the tortoise is ahead. Some reply that the premise quietly restricts our attention to the period before the catch and so cannot tell us what happens at it.
steps.ob_zh: 只要烏龜還在前面，這就是真的。有人回應說：這個前提悄悄把我們的注意力限制在「追上之前」那段時間，所以它無法告訴我們追上的那一刻發生了什麼。

steps.en: So before he catches it, Achilles must complete infinitely many runs, one after another.
steps.zh: 所以在追上之前，阿基里斯必須一個接一個，完成無窮多段的跑。
steps.ob_en: Aristotle attacked here. The stretches are only potentially infinite, he said: the run is one continuous motion, and it is we who divide it in thought. If space and time were made of smallest units, the division would also come to an end, though Zeno had other arguments against that view.
steps.ob_zh: 亞里斯多德攻擊的是這裡。他說，這些段落只是「潛在地」無窮：跑步是一個連續的運動，是我們在思想裡把它切開的。如果空間與時間由最小單位構成，分割也會有盡頭；不過芝諾另有論證反對那種看法。

steps.en: No one can complete infinitely many runs in a finite time.
steps.zh: 沒有人能在有限的時間內完成無窮多段的跑。
steps.ob_en: This is the step most often attacked. If each run takes a tenth of the time of the one before, the times form a series with a finite sum, 11.11… seconds. The premise treats “infinitely many” as if it meant “infinitely long.” Whether a finite sum fully explains how an endless sequence gets finished is the point Thomson and others have pressed.
steps.ob_zh: 這是最常被攻擊的一步。如果每一段所花的時間是前一段的十分之一，這些時間構成一個總和有限的級數：11.11… 秒。這個前提把「無窮多」當成了「無窮長」。至於一個有限的總和，是否就完全解釋了一個沒有盡頭的序列怎麼被做完，那正是湯姆森等人追問的地方。

steps.en: Therefore Achilles never catches the tortoise.
steps.zh: 所以阿基里斯永遠追不上烏龜。
steps.ob_en: Zeno accepted the conclusion, or something stronger: that motion itself is not real. Almost everyone since has taken the argument as a reductio of one of its premises. The interest lies in the disagreement about which.
steps.ob_zh: 芝諾接受這個結論，或者說接受一個更強的結論：運動本身不是真實的。此後幾乎所有人都把這個論證看成對它某個前提的歸謬。有意思的地方在於，大家對「是哪一個」意見不一。

source.work_zh: 亞里斯多德《物理學》卷六第九章；《莊子・天下》
source.tr: Aristotle translated by R. P. Hardie and R. K. Gaye (public domain); the Zhuangzi line in our own translation
source.lead_en: Zeno’s book is lost. Everything we know of his arguments comes from later writers, and chiefly from Aristotle, who reports them in order to refute them.
source.lead_zh: 芝諾的書失傳了。我們對他論證的了解全部來自後來的作者，主要是亞里斯多德；而亞里斯多德記下它們，是為了反駁。

passages.en: The second is the so-called ‘Achilles’, and it amounts to this, that in a race the quickest runner can never overtake the slowest, since the pursuer must first reach the point whence the pursued started, so that the slower must always hold a lead.
passages.zh: 第二個是所謂的「阿基里斯」，它的大意是：在賽跑中，跑得最快的永遠追不上最慢的，因為追的人必須先到達被追的人出發的那一點，所以慢的那個必定一直保持領先。
passages.note_en: Three things to notice. “So-called” shows that the argument already had its nickname in Aristotle’s day. There is no tortoise: the text says only “the slowest.” And the whole argument is a single sentence, which means that the four-premise version above is a reconstruction. Reconstructing an argument from a hostile summary is a large part of what historians of philosophy do. (“Whence” means “from which.”)
passages.note_zh: 有三件事值得注意。「所謂的」表示這個論證在亞里斯多德的時代已經有了綽號。裡面沒有烏龜：原文只說「最慢的」。而整個論證只有一句話；也就是說，上面那個四個前提的版本是重建出來的。從一份帶有敵意的摘要重建論證，是哲學史家工作的一大部分。（whence 是「從那裡」的意思。）

passages.en: A stick one foot long: take away half of it every day, and in ten thousand generations it will not be used up.
passages.zh: 一尺之捶，日取其半，萬世不竭。
passages.note_en: The line appears in a list of twenty-one sayings with which the debaters “responded to Hui Shi.” No argument is given for any of them. The Greek paradox comes down to us with its reasoning and without its author’s book, and the Chinese one with a bare conclusion, so that we have to supply the reasoning ourselves. The author of the chapter was not impressed: such men, he says, could defeat people’s mouths and could not win their hearts.
passages.note_zh: 這句話出現在辯者「與惠施相應」的二十一條說法當中，沒有一條附上論證。希臘的悖論傳到我們手上，有推理而沒有作者的書；中國的這一條只有光禿禿的結論，推理得由我們自己補。寫這一篇的人對他們不以為然：他說這些人「能勝人之口，不能服人之心」。

items.o_en: Calculus solved Zeno’s paradoxes long ago. Only philosophers still pretend there is a problem.
items.o_zh: 微積分早就解決了芝諾的悖論。只有哲學家還在假裝這裡有問題。
items.r_en: Calculus shows that the infinite series has a finite sum, and so refutes the premise that infinitely many runs need infinite time. It does not by itself show that physical space and time are infinitely divisible, as the mathematics assumes, and it does not say what it is to complete a sequence with no last step. One may think those further questions have good answers. They are still questions, and they are not answered by doing the sum.
items.r_zh: 微積分證明了這個無窮級數有有限的總和，因此駁倒了「無窮多段的跑需要無窮長的時間」這個前提。但它本身並沒有證明物理的空間與時間像數學所假定的那樣可以無限分割，也沒有說明「做完一個沒有最後一步的序列」是怎麼一回事。你可以認為這些進一步的問題都有好答案。它們仍然是問題，而且不是算出總和就回答了的。

items.o_en: The Liar is not a real sentence. A sentence that talks about itself says nothing, so it is neither true nor false and there is no paradox.
items.o_zh: 說謊者根本不是真正的句子。一個談論自己的句子什麼也沒說，所以它既不真也不假，沒有悖論可言。
items.r_en: Self-reference as such is harmless: “This sentence has five words” is plainly true. And the proposed way out leads straight back in. Take the sentence “This sentence is not true.” If it is neither true nor false, then it is not true, which is just what it says, so it is true after all. This “strengthened Liar” has defeated a long line of solutions.
items.r_zh: 自我指涉本身是無害的：「這個句子有八個字」明明白白是真的。而且這條出路會直接繞回原地。看這個句子：「這個句子不是真的。」如果它既不真也不假，那麼它就不是真的，而這正是它說的，所以它終究是真的。這個「強化版說謊者」已經打敗了一長串的解法。

items.o_en: Paradoxes are games with words. Nobody doubts that runners overtake one another or that heaps exist, so nothing is at stake.
items.o_zh: 悖論是文字遊戲。沒有人懷疑跑者會互相超越，也沒有人懷疑沙堆存在，所以這裡沒有什麼要緊的東西。
items.r_en: Nobody doubts the conclusions are false. What is in doubt is which of our own premises is to blame, and finding out has repeatedly been productive: the theory of limits, modern set theory, and Gödel’s theorems all grew out of taking a paradox seriously. The sorites is also a practical matter. Any law that fixes an age of majority or a speed limit has drawn a sharp line through a vague concept.
items.r_zh: 沒有人懷疑那些結論是假的。有疑問的是：該怪我們自己的哪一個前提？而把這件事弄清楚，一再帶來成果：極限理論、現代集合論、哥德爾定理，都是認真對待某個悖論之後長出來的。堆垛悖論也是很實際的事。任何規定成年年齡或速限的法律，都是在一個模糊的概念上畫了一條清楚的線。

said.claim: Zeno set Achilles to race against a tortoise.
said.claim_zh: 芝諾讓阿基里斯跟一隻烏龜賽跑。
said.en: Our earliest source, Aristotle, mentions no tortoise. He says only that the quickest runner cannot overtake the slowest, and the name “Achilles” tells us who the quick one was. The tortoise appears in later commentators and has been in every retelling since. Zeno’s own words are lost, so we cannot say what example he used.
said.zh: 我們最早的史料亞里斯多德並沒有提到烏龜。他只說跑得最快的追不上最慢的，而「阿基里斯」這個名字告訴我們快的那個是誰。烏龜出現在後來的註釋者筆下，從此每一次轉述都有牠。芝諾自己的話已經失傳，所以我們沒辦法說他用的是什麼例子。

terms.d_en: An apparently sound argument for an unacceptable conclusion.
terms.d_zh: 一個看來健全的論證，卻導出無法接受的結論。

terms.d_en: Refuting a claim by deriving an absurdity from it. Zeno used it against the belief in motion.
terms.d_zh: 從一個主張推出荒謬，藉此反駁它。芝諾用它來反對「運動存在」這個信念。

terms.d_en: The value that the partial sums of a series approach as closely as one likes.
terms.d_zh: 一個級數的部分和可以任意接近的那個值。

terms.d_en: An infinite series whose partial sums have a finite limit.
terms.d_zh: 部分和有有限極限的無窮級數。

terms.d_en: An infinite sequence of tasks completed in a finite time.
terms.d_zh: 在有限時間內完成的無窮多個任務。

terms.d_en: A sentence’s referring to itself, as in the Liar.
terms.d_zh: 句子指涉它自己，例如說謊者悖論。

terms.d_en: A language used to talk about another language, including about which of its sentences are true.
terms.d_zh: 用來談論另一個語言的語言，包括談論後者哪些句子為真。

terms.d_en: A paradox that proceeds by many small, individually harmless steps.
terms.d_zh: 靠許多個別看來無害的小步驟推進的悖論。

terms.d_en: The feature of a word that has borderline cases and no sharp boundary.
terms.d_zh: 一個詞有邊界個案、卻沒有明確界線的特性。

vocab.eg: Since a sound argument cannot have a false conclusion, something must give way.
vocab.eg_zh: 既然健全的論證不可能有假的結論，總得有什麼東西讓步。

vocab.zh: 硬著頭皮接受（不討喜的結論）
vocab.eg: Philosophers call accepting the incredible conclusion biting the bullet.
vocab.eg_zh: 哲學家把接受那個難以置信的結論叫作「咬子彈」。

vocab.eg: The quickest runner can never overtake the slowest.
vocab.eg_zh: 跑得最快的永遠追不上最慢的。

vocab.eg: By the time Achilles has covered the hundred, the other has crept forward ten.
vocab.eg_zh: 等阿基里斯跑完這一百公尺，對方已經往前爬了十公尺。

vocab.eg: Achilles is always on the point of drawing level and never does.
vocab.eg_zh: 阿基里斯永遠就要追平，卻永遠沒有追平。

vocab.eg: Infinitely many distances need not add up to an infinite amount.
vocab.eg_zh: 無窮多段距離，加起來不必是無窮大。

vocab.eg: Many philosophers think this dissolves the paradox.
vocab.eg_zh: 許多哲學家認為這樣就化解了悖論。

vocab.eg: What is at stake is whether space and time are as the mathematics describes them.
vocab.eg_zh: 真正牽涉到的是：空間與時間是不是像數學所描述的那樣。

vocab.eg: The same structure turned up in the foundations of mathematics.
vocab.eg_zh: 同一種結構出現在數學的基礎裡。

vocab.eg: Ordinary English falls short of that standard.
vocab.eg_zh: 日常的英語達不到那個標準。

quiz.q: According to the essay, what are the three possible responses to a paradox?
options: Reject a premise, reject a step, or accept the conclusion.
Ignore it, laugh at it, or change the subject.
Translate it, date it, or attribute it.
Prove it, publish it, or teach it.

quiz.q: Which assumption of Zeno’s does the mathematics of limits refute?
options: That infinitely many intervals must add up to an infinite total.
That Achilles is faster than the tortoise.
That the tortoise has a head start.
That a line can be divided.

quiz.q: What is Thomson’s lamp meant to show?
options: That completing infinitely many tasks may be impossible even when the times have a finite sum.
That electricity was unknown to the Greeks.
That the series one half plus one quarter and so on has no sum.
That lamps cannot be switched quickly.

quiz.q: How did Tarski respond to the Liar?
options: No language can contain its own truth predicate.
The Liar is simply false.
Sentences cannot refer to anything.
Truth does not exist.

quiz.q: Why does the essay call the sorites a practical matter?
options: Laws must draw sharp lines through vague concepts.
Sand is used in building.
Heaps are difficult to count.
Greek merchants sold grain by the heap.

write.en: Which premise of the Achilles would you reject, and why? Answer in about 150 words, and say what your answer commits you to believing about space and time.
write.zh: 阿基里斯論證的哪一個前提你會否定？為什麼？用大約 150 個英文字回答，並說明你的答案讓你對空間與時間必須相信什麼。

write.en: Run a sorites argument on a word that matters to you, such as “adult,” “fluent,” or “rich.” Where would you draw the line, and can you defend drawing it there and not one step earlier?
write.zh: 拿一個對你重要的詞（例如「成年」「流利」「有錢」）跑一次堆垛論證。你會把線畫在哪裡？你能為「畫在這裡、而不是早一步」辯護嗎？

write.en: “This sentence is false.” Explain to a friend, in plain English and without technical terms, why it is a problem.
write.zh: 「這個句子是假的。」用淺白的英文、不用術語，向朋友解釋為什麼這是個問題。

paras.en: Around 200 CE the Indian philosopher Nāgārjuna opened the second chapter of his Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way with an argument that could be mistaken for Zeno’s. What has already been traversed is not being traversed. What has not yet been traversed is not being traversed. And apart from these two there is no third stretch, “being traversed now,” to be found. In Kumārajīva’s Chinese: 已去無有去，未去亦無去，離已去未去，去時亦無去. Two centuries later his Chinese follower Sengzhao drew the conclusion in a famous line: the whirlwind that topples mountains is forever still, and the rivers that race to the sea do not flow.
paras.zh: 大約西元 200 年，印度哲學家龍樹在《中論》第二品開頭提出了一個論證，很容易被誤認成芝諾的。已經走過的路段，不是「正在走」的。還沒走到的路段，也不是「正在走」的。而在這兩者之外，找不到第三段「此刻正在走」的路。鳩摩羅什的漢譯是：「已去無有去，未去亦無去，離已去未去，去時亦無去。」兩個世紀後，他的中國後學僧肇在一句名言裡引出結論：「旋嵐偃嶽而常靜，江河兢注而不流。」

paras.en: The resemblance is real and the purposes are opposite. Zeno argued against motion in order to defend Parmenides’ single unchanging reality. Nāgārjuna has no such reality to defend. His target is the assumption that a mover, a motion, and a path each exist with a nature of their own (svabhāva); grant that assumption, he argues, and motion becomes impossible, so the assumption has to go. People walk, conventionally speaking, and nothing in the argument denies it. Where Zeno accepts the conclusion and gives up change, Nāgārjuna uses the same kind of reductio to give up fixed essences, and that leaves him with a world in which there is nothing except change. Of the three responses to a paradox, he makes the first, and the premise he rejects is one that most of his readers had never noticed they held (Dharma and the West, D8 and D9).
paras.zh: 相似是真的，目的卻相反。芝諾反對運動，是為了捍衛巴門尼德那個唯一而不變的實在。龍樹沒有這樣的實在要捍衛。他瞄準的是一個預設：行走的人、行走這件事、所走的路，各自有它自己的本性（自性，svabhāva）。他論證說，一旦承認這個預設，運動就變得不可能，所以該放棄的是這個預設。就世俗的說法而言，人是會走路的，這個論證絲毫沒有否認這一點。芝諾接受結論而放棄了變化；龍樹用同一種歸謬法放棄的是固定的本質，結果留給他的是一個除了變化別無他物的世界。在回應悖論的三種方式裡，他採取的是第一種；而他否定的那個前提，是大多數讀者從沒察覺自己抱持著的（佛法與西方哲學 D8、D9）。

further.t: Aristotle, Physics, Book VI, chapter 9, translated by R. P. Hardie and R. K. Gaye
further.n_en: All four of Zeno’s arguments about motion, in two pages.
further.n_zh: 芝諾關於運動的四個論證，兩頁之內全部交代。

further.t: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Zeno’s Paradoxes”
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Liar Paradox” and “Sorites Paradox”
R. M. Sainsbury, Paradoxes (3rd edition, 2009)
further.n_en: The standard introduction; one chapter for each family.
further.n_zh: 標準的入門書；每個家族一章。

further.t: Nāgārjuna, Mūlamadhyamakakārikā, chapter 2; see the Stanford Encyclopedia entry “Nāgārjuna”

lessons.title: How Do You Know You Are Not Dreaming?
lessons.title_zh: 你怎麼知道現在不是在作夢？
lessons.blurb_en: Descartes’ method of doubt, Zhuangzi’s butterfly, and the one belief that survives when everything else has been called into question.
lessons.blurb_zh: 笛卡兒的懷疑方法、莊周的蝴蝶，以及當其他一切都受到質疑之後，唯一留下來的那個信念。
lessons.big_en: Nothing in an experience certifies that it is not a dream. The skeptic concludes that we know nothing about the world; most of the replies give up the idea that knowledge requires certainty.
lessons.big_zh: 經驗本身沒有任何東西能保證它不是夢。懷疑論者由此推出，我們對世界一無所知；而大多數的回應，放棄的是「知識需要確定性」這個想法。

paras.en: Everyone has had the experience of waking and finding that what seemed real a moment ago was not. While it lasted, the dream did not feel like a dream. The falling felt like falling, and the examination for which one had not prepared was as alarming as a real one. This raises a question that sounds childish and turns out to be very hard. If a dream can be that convincing from the inside, what tells you that you are awake now? Whatever test you propose, pinching yourself, checking a clock, asking a friend, you could dream that you performed it and dream that you passed.
paras.zh: 每個人都有過這種經驗：醒過來，發現片刻之前看似真實的東西並不是真的。夢還在做的時候，感覺並不像夢。墜落的感覺就是墜落；那場沒準備的考試，跟真的考試一樣令人驚慌。這引出一個聽來幼稚、其實極難的問題：如果夢從裡面看可以那麼逼真，是什麼告訴你，你現在是醒著的？不管你提出什麼檢驗——捏自己一下、看時鐘、問朋友——你都可能是夢見自己做了這個檢驗，並且夢見自己通過了。

paras.en: René Descartes made this question the starting point of modern philosophy. In the Meditations of 1641 he describes himself as a man who has noticed how many false opinions he took for granted in his youth, and who resolves, once in his life, to demolish everything and begin again from the foundations. His instrument is doubt, used as a test. He will set aside any belief for which he can find the slightest ground of doubt, in order to see whether anything is left. It is important to understand that he does not think his beliefs are false. He treats them the way one treats a basket of apples when some may be rotten: tip them all out, and put back only those that pass inspection.
paras.zh: 笛卡兒把這個問題變成了近代哲學的起點。在 1641 年的《沉思集》裡，他描述自己是這樣一個人：他注意到自己年輕時把多少錯誤的意見視為理所當然，於是決心一生一次，把一切拆毀，從地基重新開始。他的工具是懷疑，拿來當作一種檢驗。任何信念，只要他找得到一絲懷疑的理由，就先擱在一邊，看看最後還剩下什麼。要緊的是明白：他並不認為自己的信念是假的。他對待它們的方式，就像對待一籃可能有幾顆爛掉的蘋果：全部倒出來，只把通過檢查的放回去。

paras.en: The doubt comes in three waves, each stronger than the last. First, the senses sometimes deceive: a square tower looks round from far away. But this touches only what is distant or small. It gives no reason to doubt, as he says, “that I am in this place, seated by the fire, clothed in a winter dressing gown.” The second wave reaches that as well. He has often dreamed of sitting by the fire while he lay undressed in bed, and on reflection he finds “that there exist no certain marks by which the state of waking can ever be distinguished from sleep.”
paras.zh: 懷疑分三波而來，一波比一波強。第一波：感官有時會騙人，方塔從遠處看是圓的。但這只碰得到遠的或小的東西；它並沒有給人理由去懷疑，如他所說，「我在這個地方，坐在爐火旁，穿著冬天的睡袍」。第二波連這一點也淹過去了。他常常夢見自己坐在爐火旁，其實當時正脫了衣服躺在床上；細想之下他發現：「沒有任何確定的標記，可以把清醒的狀態跟睡眠區分開來。」

paras.en: Even so, something seems to hold out against the dream. Whether he is awake or asleep, “two and three make five, and … a square has but four sides.” For these he needs a third and more radical supposition: that “some malignant demon, who is at once exceedingly potent and deceitful, has employed all his artifice to deceive me,” so that he goes wrong even when he adds. Nobody believes in the demon, and Descartes did not either. Its job is to mark the outer limit of what can coherently be doubted.
paras.zh: 即便如此，似乎還有東西抵擋得住夢。不管他是醒是睡，「二加三等於五，……正方形只有四條邊」。要動搖這些，他需要第三個、更徹底的假設：有「某個邪惡的魔鬼，既極其有力又善於欺騙，用盡了他一切的手段來騙我」，以致於他連做加法都會出錯。沒有人相信這個魔鬼存在，笛卡兒自己也不信。它的任務是標出「可以前後一致地懷疑」的最外緣。

paras.en: Nearly two thousand years earlier, the Chinese philosopher Zhuangzi had told the most famous dream in literature. He dreamed he was a butterfly, fluttering about, content, with no idea that he was Zhuang Zhou. Suddenly he woke, and there he was, solidly Zhuang Zhou. “He did not know whether he was Zhou who had dreamed he was a butterfly, or a butterfly dreaming he was Zhou.”
paras.zh: 比這早將近兩千年，中國哲學家莊子講了文學史上最有名的一場夢。他夢見自己是一隻蝴蝶，翩翩飛舞，自在得意，完全不知道自己是莊周。忽然醒來，他又明明白白是莊周了。「不知周之夢為胡蝶與，胡蝶之夢為周與？」

paras.en: The premise is Descartes’ and the mood is entirely different. Descartes is alarmed and wants certainty back. Zhuangzi is unworried. He adds that between Zhou and the butterfly there must be some distinction, and calls this “the transformation of things.” Elsewhere in the same chapter he suggests that only after a great awakening will we know that all this was a great dream, while fools believe that they are already awake. For him the dream is a way of loosening our confidence in fixed distinctions: self and other, waking and sleeping, perhaps life and death.
paras.zh: 前提跟笛卡兒的一樣，心情卻完全不同。笛卡兒是驚慌的，他要把確定性找回來。莊子並不擔心。他接著說，莊周與蝴蝶之間必定有分別，並把這稱為「物化」。在同一篇的另一處他提到：要有一場大覺，然後才知道這一切是一場大夢，而愚昧的人自以為已經醒了。對莊子來說，夢是一種方法，用來鬆開我們對固定區分的信心：我與物、醒與睡，也許還有生與死。

paras.en: At the bottom of his doubt Descartes finds one thing the demon cannot take away. Let the demon deceive him as much as it can: to be deceived he must exist. “This proposition I am, I exist, is necessarily true each time it is expressed by me, or conceived in my mind.” The point is usually called the cogito, from the Latin for “I think.” Notice how little it gives him. It tells him that he exists for as long as he is thinking, and that he is at least a thing that thinks. It does not yet tell him that he has a body, that he has a past, or that anything exists outside his mind. Descartes spent the remaining four Meditations trying to win the world back, by way of a proof that God exists and is no deceiver. Few readers have been persuaded by that route. The doubt has proved more durable than the cure.
paras.zh: 在懷疑的最底層，笛卡兒找到一樣魔鬼拿不走的東西。任憑魔鬼怎麼騙他：要被騙，他就必須存在。「『我是，我存在』這個命題，每當我說出它、或在心裡想到它的時候，必然是真的。」這一點通常稱為 cogito，取自拉丁文的「我思」。注意它給他的有多麼少。它告訴他：只要他在思考，他就存在；而且他至少是一個會思考的東西。它還沒有告訴他：他有身體、他有過去，或者他的心靈之外有任何東西存在。笛卡兒用剩下的四篇沉思，試著把世界贏回來，走的是「證明上帝存在、而且不會騙人」這條路。很少讀者被這條路說服。懷疑比解藥耐久得多。

paras.en: The position that we cannot know anything about the external world is called skepticism, and three kinds of reply are worth knowing. The first is G. E. Moore’s. In a lecture of 1939 he held up his hands and said, in effect: here is one hand, and here is another; so there are external things. He granted that he could not prove he was not dreaming. His point was that he was far more certain of his hands than he could ever be of the premises of any philosophical argument to the contrary, so it was the argument that had to go.
paras.zh: 主張我們對外在世界一無所知的立場，稱為懷疑論；有三類回應值得知道。第一類是摩爾的。在 1939 年的一場演講裡，他舉起雙手，大意是說：這裡有一隻手，這裡還有一隻；所以外在的東西是存在的。他承認自己無法證明不是在作夢。他的重點是：他對自己雙手的確定程度，遠遠超過他對任何相反的哲學論證之前提所能有的確定程度；所以該被放棄的是那個論證。

paras.en: The second reply denies that knowledge requires certainty. On this view, called fallibilism, I know that I am awake if my belief is true and is produced in a reliable way, even though I cannot rule out every imaginable alternative. For all I know in the skeptic’s sense, I might be dreaming; in the ordinary sense, I know perfectly well that I am not. The third reply questions whether the skeptic’s story makes sense. Hilary Putnam argued in 1981 that a brain which had always been kept in a vat and fed its experiences by a computer could not even think the thought “I am a brain in a vat,” because its words would never have been connected to real brains and vats. None of these replies is accepted by everyone, which is why the dream is still discussed in every introductory course.
paras.zh: 第二類回應否認知識需要確定性。照這個稱為「可錯論」的看法，只要我的信念為真，而且是以可靠的方式產生的，我就「知道」我醒著，儘管我無法排除每一個想像得到的其他可能。照懷疑論者的意思，就我所知，我有可能在作夢；照日常的意思，我清清楚楚知道我沒有。第三類回應質疑懷疑論者的故事到底說不說得通。普特南在 1981 年論證：一顆從來就被養在桶子裡、由電腦餵給它種種經驗的大腦，連「我是一顆桶中之腦」這個想法都想不出來，因為它的字詞從來沒有跟真正的腦與桶子連結過。這些回應沒有一個是人人接受的；所以每一門哲學導論，至今還在討論那場夢。

paras.en: It is tempting to say that none of this could make any practical difference, and in one sense that is true. You will not tell dreaming and waking apart any better after reading Descartes. What changes is your picture of what knowing is. Before the dream argument it is natural to think of knowledge as a direct grasp of how things are. After it, one has to choose. Either knowledge demands a certainty that almost nothing can meet, or it is something more modest: true belief that is well supported and could, in principle, have been wrong. Most philosophers today take the second view. So do the sciences, which hold even their best theories open to revision. The dream argument is where that modesty was first learned.
paras.zh: 人很容易說：這一切不可能造成任何實際的差別。在某個意義上這是真的。讀完笛卡兒，你分辨夢與醒的能力並不會變好。改變的是你對「知道」是怎麼回事的圖像。在夢的論證之前，人很自然地把知識想成對事物實況的直接掌握。在那之後，你必須做選擇：要嘛知識要求一種幾乎沒有東西達得到的確定性；要嘛知識是比較謙遜的東西——有良好根據的真信念，而且原則上本來有可能是錯的。今天多數的哲學家採取第二種看法。科學也是如此：即使是最好的理論，科學也保留修正的餘地。這份謙遜，最早就是從夢的論證學來的。

lab.title_en: Try it: the ladder of doubt
lab.title_zh: 親手做一次：懷疑的階梯
lab.lead_en: Ten things you are sure of. Before each of Descartes’ three waves, mark the beliefs you expect it to knock down, then apply the doubt and see whether you and Descartes agree.
lab.lead_zh: 十件你確定的事。在笛卡兒的三波懷疑每一波來之前，先標出你預期會被沖倒的信念，再施加懷疑，看看你跟笛卡兒的判斷一不一樣。

t.en: That tower in the distance is round.
t.zh: 遠方那座塔是圓的。

t.en: The voice calling across the valley is my friend’s.
t.zh: 山谷對面喊我的聲音，是我朋友的。

t.en: I am sitting here, reading this page.
t.zh: 我正坐在這裡讀這一頁。

t.en: I have two hands.
t.zh: 我有兩隻手。

t.en: There is a world of physical things outside my mind.
t.zh: 我的心靈之外，有一個由物體構成的世界。

t.en: There are other minds besides my own.
t.zh: 除了我之外，還有別的心靈。

t.en: Two and three make five.
t.zh: 二加三等於五。

t.en: A square has four sides.
t.zh: 正方形有四條邊。

t.en: I am thinking right now.
t.zh: 我此刻正在思考。

t.en: I exist.
t.zh: 我存在。

q.en: My senses have misled me before, about things that were far away or very small. Which beliefs does that put in doubt?
q.zh: 我的感官以前騙過我，在很遠或很小的東西上。這讓哪些信念變得可疑？

why.en: Only the two that depend on perceiving something distant fall. Descartes says it would be mad to doubt, on these grounds alone, that he is sitting by the fire. Arithmetic and his own existence are untouched.
why.zh: 只有那兩個依賴「感知遠處事物」的信念倒下。笛卡兒說，單憑這個理由就懷疑自己坐在爐火旁，那是瘋了。算術與他自己的存在毫髮無傷。

q.en: In dreams I have been just as sure that I was up and dressed. There are no certain marks to tell waking from sleep. What falls now?
q.zh: 在夢裡，我同樣確信自己起了床、穿好了衣服。沒有確定的標記可以分辨醒與睡。現在倒下的是哪些？

why.en: Everything about my present surroundings and my own body falls. Descartes holds that the simple truths of arithmetic and geometry still stand, since two and three make five whether I am awake or asleep. He does not yet doubt that a world of some kind exists, because dreams are made out of materials taken from somewhere.
why.zh: 關於我當下的環境與我自己身體的一切都倒了。笛卡兒認為算術與幾何的簡單真理依然站著，因為不管我醒著還是睡著，二加三都等於五。他這時還沒有懷疑「有某種世界存在」，因為夢是用從某處取來的材料做成的。

q.en: Suppose a being of great power devotes itself to deceiving me, even when I count the sides of a square. What can still stand?
q.zh: 假設有一個法力強大的存在，一心一意要騙我，連我數正方形的邊的時候也不放過。還有什麼站得住？

why.en: The external world, other minds, and mathematics all fall. Two beliefs cannot: to be deceived I must be thinking, and to be thinking I must exist. This is the cogito.
why.zh: 外在世界、他人的心靈、數學全都倒了。有兩個信念倒不了：要被騙，我必須在思考；要思考，我必須存在。這就是 cogito。

end.en: Two beliefs out of ten are left. Descartes thought he could rebuild everything from them. Most philosophers think he could not, and have looked for a way of knowing that does not need a foundation this narrow.
end.zh: 十個信念剩下兩個。笛卡兒認為他可以從這兩個重建一切。多數哲學家認為他辦不到，轉而尋找一種不需要這麼窄的地基的「知道」。

argument.lead_en: The skeptic’s reasoning is short and valid. It is modus tollens, and each premise seems hard to deny. Click a step to see what can be said against it.
argument.lead_zh: 懷疑論者的推理很短，而且有效。它是一個否定後件，每個前提看來都很難否認。點任何一步，看看別人可以怎麼反對它。

steps.en: If I know that I am reading a page, then I know that I am not merely dreaming that I am reading one.
steps.zh: 如果我知道我正在讀一頁文字，那麼我就知道我不只是「夢見」自己在讀。
steps.ob_en: This rests on the closure principle: if you know one thing, and know that it entails a second, you know the second. Fred Dretske and Robert Nozick denied closure. On their view I can know that I am reading without knowing that the far-fetched alternatives are false. Critics find that hard to accept, since it allows me to say “I know I am reading, but I do not know that I am not dreaming.”
steps.ob_zh: 這個前提靠的是「封閉原則」：如果你知道一件事，又知道它蘊涵第二件事，你就知道第二件事。德雷斯基與諾齊克否定封閉原則。照他們的看法，我可以知道我在讀，而不必知道那些牽強的其他可能是假的。批評者覺得這很難接受，因為它容許我說：「我知道我在讀，但我不知道我不是在作夢。」

steps.en: I do not know that I am not dreaming, since any evidence I have could itself be part of a dream.
steps.zh: 我不知道我不是在作夢，因為我擁有的任何證據，本身都可能是夢的一部分。
steps.ob_en: This is the step most often attacked. It assumes that to know something I must be able to rule out every possibility of error by evidence available from the inside. The fallibilist replies that knowledge requires only a true belief formed in a reliable way. If I am in fact awake and my senses are working, I know it, whether or not I can prove it to a skeptic.
steps.ob_zh: 這是最常被攻擊的一步。它預設：要知道一件事，我必須能憑著「從裡面拿得到」的證據，排除每一種出錯的可能。可錯論者回答：知識只需要一個以可靠方式形成的真信念。如果我事實上醒著，我的感官也運作正常，我就知道我醒著，不管我能不能向懷疑論者證明。

steps.en: Therefore I do not know that I am reading a page.
steps.zh: 所以，我不知道我正在讀一頁文字。
steps.ob_en: Moore ran the argument in reverse. I do know that I am reading; so, by the first premise, I know that I am not dreaming. The logic is equally valid in both directions. The question is which you are more sure of, the skeptic’s second premise or your own hands. Philosophers say that one person’s modus tollens is another’s modus ponens.
steps.ob_zh: 摩爾把這個論證倒過來跑：我確實知道我在讀；所以依第一個前提，我知道我不是在作夢。兩個方向的邏輯同樣有效。問題在於你對哪一個更有把握：懷疑論者的第二個前提，還是你自己的雙手。哲學家有句話說：一個人的否定後件，是另一個人的肯定前件。

source.work: René Descartes, Meditations on First Philosophy (1641), I and II
source.work_zh: 笛卡兒《第一哲學沉思集》第一、二沉思
source.lead_en: The Meditations is written in the first person and is meant to be performed. The reader is supposed to go through the doubt personally, one day at a time, as the author did.
source.lead_zh: 《沉思集》用第一人稱寫成，是要讓人「照著做」的。讀者應當像作者那樣，一天一篇，親自把懷疑走過一遍。

passages.en: I perceive so clearly that there exist no certain marks by which the state of waking can ever be distinguished from sleep, that I feel greatly astonished; and in amazement I almost persuade myself that I am now dreaming.
passages.zh: 我如此清楚地察覺到，並沒有任何確定的標記可以把清醒的狀態跟睡眠區分開來，以致於我大為驚愕；在驚愕之中，我幾乎要說服自己：我此刻正在作夢。
passages.note_en: The claim is narrower than it is usually reported to be. He does not say that waking and dreaming feel the same. He says there are no certain marks, that is, no feature of an experience that could not also occur in a dream. Look too at the word “almost.” The Meditations records a real exercise, and he reports its effect on him with some care.
passages.note_zh: 這個主張比一般轉述的要窄。他沒有說醒與夢「感覺起來一樣」。他說的是沒有「確定的標記」，也就是說，經驗沒有哪一項特徵是夢裡不可能也出現的。也看看「幾乎」這個詞。《沉思集》記錄的是一場真實的練習，他相當仔細地報告了這場練習對他的作用。

passages.en: So that it must, in fine, be maintained, all things being maturely and carefully considered, that this proposition (pronunciatum) I am, I exist, is necessarily true each time it is expressed by me, or conceived in my mind.
passages.zh: 所以，把一切成熟而仔細地考慮過之後，終究必須主張：「我是，我存在」這個命題，每當我說出它、或在心裡想到它的時候，必然是真的。
passages.note_en: Two details matter. There is no “therefore”: he does not present his existence as the conclusion of an inference from “I think.” And the certainty is tied to the moment, “each time it is expressed.” It is the certainty of a performance, something like the truth of “I am speaking” while one is speaking. (“In fine” is an old phrase for “in short.”)
passages.note_zh: 有兩個細節很重要。這裡沒有「所以」：他並沒有把自己的存在，說成是從「我思」推論出來的結論。而且這份確定性是綁在當下的：「每當我說出它的時候」。它是一種「做出來」的確定性，有點像一個人在說話的時候，「我正在說話」這句話為真。（in fine 是舊式用語，意思是「總之」。）

items.o_en: Dreams and waking life are easy to tell apart. Dreams are patchy and disconnected, and waking life hangs together from one day to the next.
items.o_zh: 夢跟清醒的生活很容易分辨。夢是零碎而不連貫的；清醒的生活一天接一天，前後連得起來。
items.r_en: This is Descartes’ own answer at the end of the Sixth Meditation, and as a practical test it is sound. It has two limits. It can be applied only afterward, from a standpoint already taken to be waking. And it does nothing against the demon, or its modern descendants the brain in a vat and the computer simulation, which are designed to be perfectly coherent.
items.r_zh: 這是笛卡兒自己在第六沉思結尾給的答案；當作實用的檢驗，它是站得住的。它有兩個限制。它只能事後運用，而且是從一個已經被當作「醒著」的立足點來運用。它對魔鬼也毫無作用；對魔鬼的現代後裔——桶中之腦與電腦模擬——同樣如此，因為這些假設本來就被設計成完全連貫。

items.o_en: The doubt is a pretense. Nobody can actually doubt that he has hands, so nothing follows from saying that one does.
items.o_zh: 這種懷疑是裝出來的。沒有人真的能懷疑自己有手；所以嘴上說懷疑，推不出任何東西。
items.r_en: Hume observed that skeptical doubts vanish as soon as he left his study, and the American philosopher C. S. Peirce later insisted that we should not pretend to doubt in philosophy what we do not doubt in our hearts. Descartes would agree that the doubt is artificial. His question was never whether we do believe these things. It was what entitles us to, and that question is not answered by pointing out that we cannot help it.
items.r_zh: 休謨說過，他一走出書房，懷疑論的疑慮就煙消雲散；美國哲學家皮爾士後來堅持，我們不該在哲學裡假裝懷疑自己心裡並不懷疑的事。笛卡兒會同意這種懷疑是人為的。他的問題從來不是我們「是否」相信這些事，而是我們「憑什麼有資格」相信；指出我們不由自主地相信，並沒有回答這個問題。

items.o_en: The cogito proves less than Descartes claims. From the fact that there is thinking, it does not follow that there is an “I” who does it.
items.o_zh: Cogito 證明的比笛卡兒宣稱的少。從「有思考在進行」這個事實，推不出有一個在思考的「我」。
items.r_en: The eighteenth-century physicist Georg Lichtenberg made the objection in a sentence: one should say “it thinks,” in the way one says “there is lightning.” Descartes assumed that a thought needs a thinker, a lasting substance to which it belongs, and that assumption was never put through the doubt. This is the most serious objection of the three, and Buddhist philosophers had been pressing it for two thousand years (see below).
items.r_zh: 十八世紀的物理學家利希滕貝格用一句話提出了這個反駁：我們應該說「在思考」，就像我們說「在閃電」一樣。笛卡兒預設了思想需要一個思想者，一個它所歸屬的持存實體；而這個預設從來沒有被拿去接受懷疑的檢驗。這是三個反駁裡最嚴重的一個，而佛教哲學家已經追問了它兩千年（見下文）。

said.claim: “I think, therefore I am” is the famous line of the Meditations.
said.claim_zh: 「我思故我在」是《沉思集》裡的名句。
said.en: The sentence comes from the Discourse on Method (1637), written in French: je pense, donc je suis. The Latin cogito, ergo sum appears in the Principles of Philosophy (1644). In the Meditations, his most careful treatment, Descartes writes only “I am, I exist,” with no “therefore,” perhaps to avoid the suggestion that his existence is inferred from a premise.
said.zh: 這句話出自用法文寫的《談談方法》（1637）：je pense, donc je suis。拉丁文的 cogito, ergo sum 出現在《哲學原理》（1644）。在處理得最仔細的《沉思集》裡，笛卡兒只寫「我是，我存在」，沒有「所以」；也許是為了避免讓人以為，他的存在是從某個前提推論出來的。

terms.d_en: The view that we lack knowledge in some domain, here knowledge of the external world.
terms.d_zh: 主張我們在某個領域缺乏知識的看法；這裡指的是對外在世界的知識。

terms.d_en: Descartes’ procedure of setting aside every belief that can be doubted, in order to find what cannot.
terms.d_zh: 笛卡兒的做法：把一切可以懷疑的信念擱在一邊，以找出無法懷疑的。

terms.d_en: The insight that I cannot doubt my own existence while I am thinking.
terms.d_zh: 這個洞見：在我思考的時候，我無法懷疑自己的存在。

terms.d_en: Impossible to doubt.
terms.d_zh: 不可能被懷疑的。

terms.d_en: Whatever exists outside one’s own mind.
terms.d_zh: 存在於自己心靈之外的一切。

terms.d_en: If you know P, and know that P entails Q, then you know Q.
terms.d_zh: 如果你知道 P，又知道 P 蘊涵 Q，那麼你就知道 Q。

terms.d_en: The view that one can know something without being certain of it.
terms.d_zh: 主張人可以知道一件事，而不必對它有確定性。

terms.d_en: The modern version of the demon: a brain kept alive and fed false experiences by a computer.
terms.d_zh: 魔鬼的現代版本：一顆被維持存活、由電腦餵給虛假經驗的大腦。

vocab.eg: He noticed how many false opinions he had taken for granted in his youth.
vocab.eg_zh: 他注意到自己年輕時把多少錯誤的意見視為理所當然。

vocab.eg: He resolves to demolish everything and begin again from the foundations.
vocab.eg_zh: 他決心把一切拆毀，從地基重新開始。

vocab.eg: He will set aside any belief for which he can find a ground of doubt.
vocab.eg_zh: 任何信念只要找得到懷疑的理由，他就先擱在一邊。

vocab.eg: Something seems to hold out against the dream.
vocab.eg_zh: 似乎還有東西抵擋得住夢。

vocab.eg: One belief survives when everything else has been called into question.
vocab.eg_zh: 當其他一切都受到質疑，有一個信念留了下來。

vocab.eg: He tried to win the world back by way of a proof that God exists.
vocab.eg_zh: 他試著經由「上帝存在」的證明，把世界贏回來。

vocab.eg: The doubt has proved more durable than the cure.
vocab.eg_zh: 懷疑比解藥耐久得多。

vocab.eg: For all I know, I might be dreaming.
vocab.eg_zh: 就我所知，我有可能在作夢。

vocab.eg: You will not tell dreaming and waking apart any better after reading Descartes.
vocab.eg_zh: 讀完笛卡兒，你分辨夢與醒的能力並不會變好。

vocab.eg: The sciences hold even their best theories open to revision.
vocab.eg_zh: 即使是最好的理論，科學也保留修正的餘地。

quiz.q: What is the purpose of Descartes’ doubt?
options: To test his beliefs and find out whether any is beyond doubt.
To show that all his beliefs are false.
To prove that life is a dream.
To defend the reliability of the senses.

quiz.q: Why does Descartes need the demon in addition to the dream?
options: Simple truths of arithmetic seem to hold whether one is awake or asleep.
Dreams never contain numbers.
He did not believe that people dream.
The dream argument applies only to distant objects.

quiz.q: How does Zhuangzi’s use of the dream differ from Descartes’?
options: He uses it to loosen fixed distinctions and is not seeking certainty.
He proves that he is a butterfly.
He uses it to establish that God exists.
He denies that anyone ever dreams.

quiz.q: What is Moore’s reply to the skeptic?
options: He is more certain that he has hands than of any premise in the skeptic’s argument.
He can prove that he is not dreaming.
Hands do not exist.
Certainty is impossible about anything at all.

quiz.q: What does fallibilism claim?
options: One can know something without being certain of it.
No one knows anything.
Every belief is false.
Knowledge requires ruling out every possible error.

write.en: Describe a dream that you took to be real while it lasted. Then say exactly what, if anything, is different about your experience at this moment.
write.zh: 描述一場你在做的時候信以為真的夢。然後確切地說出，你此刻的經驗跟它有什麼不同（如果有的話）。

write.en: Which reply to the skeptic do you find strongest: Moore’s, the fallibilist’s, or Putnam’s? Defend your choice in about 150 words and state the best objection to it.
write.zh: 對懷疑論者的回應，你覺得哪一個最強：摩爾的、可錯論的，還是普特南的？用大約 150 個英文字為你的選擇辯護，並說出對它最好的反駁。

write.en: Zhuangzi is untroubled by the butterfly and Descartes is alarmed by the dream. Whose attitude seems more reasonable to you, and why?
write.zh: 莊子對蝴蝶毫不在意，笛卡兒卻被夢嚇到了。你覺得誰的態度比較合理？為什麼？

paras.en: Buddhist texts reach for the dream constantly. The Diamond Sūtra ends by advising that all conditioned things be viewed “as a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow” (一切有為法，如夢幻泡影). The comparison is put to philosophical work in Vasubandhu’s Twenty Verses, written in India in the fourth or fifth century. Vasubandhu holds that what we experience is “consciousness only,” and he faces an obvious objection: if there were no external objects, why would experiences be tied to particular places and times? He answers with the dream. In a dream too we see a village or a garden at one place and not everywhere, at one time and not always, though no external village is there (處時定如夢). The orderliness of experience therefore does not prove that it has an outside cause.
paras.zh: 佛典不斷地用夢作比喻。《金剛經》的結尾勸人這樣看待一切有為法：「如夢幻泡影」。在世親的《唯識二十論》裡（西元四或五世紀作於印度），這個比喻被拿來做哲學的工作。世親主張我們所經驗到的「唯有識」，並且面對一個顯而易見的反駁：如果沒有外在的對象，經驗為什麼會固定在特定的地點與時間？他用夢來回答。在夢裡，我們同樣是在某一處、而不是處處，在某一時、而不是時時，看見村莊或園林，雖然並沒有外在的村莊在那裡（「處時定如夢」）。所以經驗的井然有序，並不能證明它有一個外在的原因。

paras.en: So far this is Descartes’ second wave. The difference lies in what follows. Descartes treats the dream as a threat and brings in God to remove it. Vasubandhu accepts the comparison and draws a practical conclusion: ordinary waking life is itself a kind of sleep, from which one can wake. That is the literal meaning of buddha, “one who has awakened,” and it is very close to Zhuangzi’s “great awakening.” On the cogito the traditions part more sharply. A Buddhist philosopher grants that thinking is going on and denies the step to a thinker. What Descartes found at the bottom of his doubt and took for a substance, the Buddhist analysis takes apart into a stream of momentary events with no owner. Lichtenberg’s objection is, in effect, the doctrine of no-self (Dharma and the West, D2 and D11).
paras.zh: 到這裡為止，這就是笛卡兒的第二波懷疑。差別在接下來的地方。笛卡兒把夢當作威脅，請出上帝來排除它。世親接受這個比擬，並且引出一個實踐上的結論：平常的清醒生活本身就是一種睡眠，而人可以從中醒來。這正是 buddha 的字面意思：「覺醒的人」；它跟莊子的「大覺」非常接近。在 cogito 上，兩個傳統分得更開。佛教哲學家承認「有思考在進行」，但否認由此跨到「有一個思考者」的那一步。笛卡兒在懷疑的最底層找到、並當成實體的那個東西，佛教的分析把它拆成一串沒有主人的剎那事件。利希滕貝格的反駁，實際上就是無我的教義（佛法與西方哲學 D2、D11）。

further.t: René Descartes, Meditations on First Philosophy, translated by John Veitch
further.n_en: The first two Meditations take an hour and are the best introduction to philosophy ever written.
further.n_zh: 前兩篇沉思一小時讀得完，是有史以來最好的哲學入門。

further.t: Zhuangzi, chapter 2, “On the Equality of Things” (齊物論)
further.n_en: The butterfly is the last paragraph; the “great awakening” comes a little earlier.
further.n_zh: 蝴蝶是最後一段；「大覺」在稍前面。

further.t: G. E. Moore, “Proof of an External World” (1939)
further.n_en: The lecture with the two hands.
further.n_zh: 舉起雙手的那場演講。

further.t: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Skepticism”
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Vasubandhu”
further.n_en: On the Twenty Verses and the dream argument.
further.n_zh: 談《唯識二十論》與夢的論證。

lessons.title: Is Seeing Believing?
lessons.blurb_en: Plato’s cave: prisoners who take shadows for reality, one who is dragged into the sun, and the question of what it would mean to see things as they are.
lessons.blurb_zh: 柏拉圖的洞穴：把影子當成實在的囚徒，一個被拖到陽光下的人，以及這個問題——「如實地看見事物」到底是什麼意思。
lessons.big_en: What the senses show us may stand to reality as a shadow stands to the thing that casts it. If so, education is a turning of the whole person toward what is real, and it will be resisted.
lessons.big_zh: 感官呈現給我們的東西，跟實在的關係，也許就像影子跟投下影子的東西。如果是這樣，教育就是把整個人轉向真實的那個過程，而這個過程會遭到抗拒。

paras.en: “Seeing is believing” is a proverb about evidence, and as a rule of thumb it is a good one. Yet the things we see are a strange guide to how the world is. The sun looks about the size of a coin and appears to cross the sky. A straight stick looks bent in water. The night sky shows stars that may have burned out long ago. In each case we have learned to correct what we see by what we understand. Plato asked how far that correction might go. Suppose that everything the senses show us is related to reality in the way that a picture of a thing is related to the thing. He put the thought in the form of a story, told by Socrates in Book VII of the Republic, and it has become the best-known image in philosophy.
paras.zh: 「眼見為憑」是一句關於證據的俗話；當作經驗法則，它是不錯的。可是我們看見的東西，對世界實際的樣子來說，是個古怪的嚮導。太陽看起來跟硬幣差不多大，而且好像橫越天空。筆直的棍子插進水裡看起來是彎的。夜空裡顯現的星星，也許早就燃盡了。在每一種情形裡，我們都學會了用「理解到的」去修正「看見的」。柏拉圖問的是：這種修正可以走到多遠？假設感官呈現給我們的一切，跟實在的關係，就像一樣東西的圖像跟那樣東西本身的關係。他把這個想法寫成一個故事，由蘇格拉底在《理想國》第七卷說出來；這個故事成了哲學裡最廣為人知的意象。

paras.en: Picture people living in an underground cave whose long entrance is open to the daylight. “Here they have been from their childhood, and have their legs and necks chained so that they cannot move, and can only see before them.” Behind and above them a fire is burning. Between the fire and the prisoners runs a raised path with a low wall along it, like the screen at a puppet show, and along the path people carry statues and figures of animals, which stick up above the wall. The firelight throws the shadows of these figures on the wall of the cave in front of the prisoners.
paras.zh: 想像有一群人住在地下的洞穴裡，洞穴有一條長長的通道通向日光。「他們從小就在這裡，腿和脖子都被鍊住，所以不能移動，只能看見前面。」在他們背後的高處，有一堆火在燒。火與囚徒之間有一條墊高的路，路邊有一道矮牆，就像木偶戲的屏幕；有人沿著這條路，搬運人像與動物的造像，這些東西高出矮牆。火光把這些造像的影子，投在囚徒面前的洞壁上。

paras.en: The prisoners have never seen anything else. They give the shadows names, and they honor whoever is quickest at predicting which shadow will come next. If the carriers speak, the echo seems to come from the shadows. “To them,” Socrates says, “the truth would be literally nothing but the shadows of the images.” His companion remarks that these are strange prisoners. Socrates answers: “Like ourselves.”
paras.zh: 囚徒從來沒有見過別的東西。他們替影子取名字，並且推崇最會預測下一個影子的人。如果搬運的人說話，回聲聽起來就像是從影子發出來的。蘇格拉底說：「對他們來說，真實簡直就只是那些造像的影子。」他的同伴說，這些囚徒真奇怪。蘇格拉底回答：「跟我們一樣。」

paras.en: Now suppose one prisoner is released and forced to stand up and turn around. The movement hurts, and the fire dazzles him. Told that what he sees now is more real than the shadows, he does not believe it, for the shadows were clear and these shapes are a blur. If he is then dragged up the steep, rough passage into the sunlight, he is at first unable to see anything at all. His eyes adjust by stages. He can look first at shadows, then at reflections in water, then at things themselves, then at the moon and stars by night. “Last of all he will be able to see the sun, and not mere reflections of him in the water.” He comes to understand that the sun produces the seasons and governs everything in the visible world, and that it is in some way the cause of all that he and his companions used to see.
paras.zh: 現在假設有一個囚徒被鬆開，被強迫站起來、轉過身去。這個動作讓他疼痛，火光讓他目眩。有人告訴他，他現在看到的比影子更真實；他不相信，因為影子是清楚的，而這些形體一片模糊。如果接著他被人拖上那條陡峭崎嶇的通道，拉到陽光下，他起初什麼也看不見。他的眼睛是一階一階適應的。他先能看影子，然後是水中的倒影，然後是事物本身，然後是夜裡的月亮與星星。「最後他將能夠看見太陽，而不只是太陽在水中的倒影。」他終於明白，是太陽造成四季、主宰可見世界裡的一切，而且在某種意義上，它是他與同伴們過去所見一切的原因。

paras.en: Socrates explains the image himself. “The prison-house is the world of sight, the light of the fire is the sun,” and the journey upward is “the ascent of the soul into the intellectual world.” So the cave is the whole world that our senses reveal, and the world outside stands for what can be grasped only by thinking. The things out there are what Plato calls Forms: justice itself, beauty itself, the triangle that geometry studies, as opposed to this or that just act, beautiful face, or chalk drawing. The sun stands for the highest of them, the Form of the Good, which, he says, “appears last of all, and is seen only with an effort.”
paras.zh: 蘇格拉底自己解釋了這個意象。「牢房就是視覺的世界，火的光就是太陽」，而向上的旅程是「靈魂上升到理智的世界」。所以洞穴就是感官向我們揭示的整個世界，洞外的世界則代表只有靠思考才能掌握的東西。外面的那些事物，就是柏拉圖所說的「理型」：正義本身、美本身、幾何學研究的那個三角形，而不是這個或那個正義的行為、美麗的臉孔、粉筆畫的圖。太陽代表其中最高的一個，「善的理型」；他說，它「最後才出現，而且要費力才看得見」。

paras.en: Why believe in such things? Plato’s main reason concerns knowledge. Whatever we perceive is changing, and it has its qualities only more or less: two sticks are equal from here and unequal from there, and a law is just in one city and unjust in another. Yet we do seem to know what equality and justice are, well enough to see that the sticks and the laws fall short. Plato concludes that knowledge must have objects of its own, stable and perfect, which particular things only resemble.
paras.zh: 為什麼要相信有這種東西？柏拉圖的主要理由跟知識有關。我們感知到的一切都在變，而且它們具有某種性質，總是只到某個程度：兩根棍子從這裡看相等，從那裡看不等；一條法律在這個城邦是正義的，在另一個城邦是不義的。然而我們似乎確實知道相等與正義是什麼，而且知道得夠清楚，才看得出那些棍子與法律有所不足。柏拉圖的結論是：知識必定有它自己的對象，穩定而完美，個別事物只是與它們相似。

paras.en: The story does not end in the sunlight. The freed prisoner remembers the others and pities them, and he goes back down. His eyes, used to the sun, are now useless in the dark. He does badly at the shadow contests. “Men would say of him that up he went and down he came without his eyes,” and that the journey is not worth making. If anyone tried to free them and lead them up, Socrates adds, they would kill him if they could. Plato’s first readers knew whom he meant. Athens had put Socrates to death some twenty years before.
paras.zh: 故事並沒有在陽光下結束。被釋放的囚徒想起其他人，憐憫他們，於是走回洞裡。他的眼睛習慣了太陽，現在在黑暗裡毫無用處。他在猜影子的比賽裡表現很差。「人們會說，他上去一趟，回來眼睛就壞了」，並且說這趟旅程根本不值得走。蘇格拉底又說，如果有人想解開他們、帶他們上去，他們要是辦得到，會把那個人殺掉。柏拉圖最早的讀者知道他指的是誰。雅典在大約二十年前處死了蘇格拉底。

paras.en: The return is also a duty. In Plato’s ideal city, those who have seen the Good are not allowed to stay above. “They must be made to descend again among the prisoners in the den, and partake of their labours and honours.” They would prefer to stay in the light, and Plato argues that this is exactly what fits them to govern.
paras.zh: 回去同時也是一項責任。在柏拉圖的理想城邦裡，見過「善」的人不准留在上面。「必須讓他們再下到洞穴的囚徒當中，分擔他們的勞苦與榮譽。」他們寧可留在光裡；柏拉圖論證說，正是這一點，使他們適合治理城邦。

paras.en: Before he leaves the image, Socrates draws a conclusion about teaching that every teacher should know. Education is not what some people say it is, putting knowledge into a soul that lacks it, “like sight into blind eyes.” The power to learn “exists in the soul already.” What is needed is a turning around: “just as the eye was unable to turn from darkness to light without the whole body, so too the instrument of knowledge can only by the movement of the whole soul be turned from the world of becoming into that of being.” On this view a teacher transmits nothing. The teacher’s work is to arrange things so that the student turns and looks. The turning is uncomfortable, and the student may well resent the person who causes it.
paras.zh: 在離開這個意象之前，蘇格拉底引出了一個關於教學的結論，每一位老師都該知道。教育並不是某些人說的那樣，把知識放進缺少知識的靈魂裡，「像把視力放進瞎了的眼睛」。學習的能力「本來就在靈魂之中」。需要的是一次轉向：「正如眼睛不連著整個身體就無法從黑暗轉向光明，認識的工具也只有藉著整個靈魂的運動，才能從生成變化的世界轉向存有的世界。」照這個看法，老師什麼也沒有傳遞。老師的工作是把事情安排好，讓學生轉過身去看。這個轉身並不舒服，而學生很可能怨恨促成它的那個人。

paras.en: Few philosophers now accept Plato’s Forms. His own pupil Aristotle argued that the form of a thing exists in the thing and cannot be found in a separate realm. But the cave has outlived the theory it was built to illustrate, because the situation it describes keeps recurring. People do mistake the images of things for things. Much of what anyone believes about the wider world was seen on a screen, arranged by people who remain out of sight behind a wall. And the story makes a point about method that does not depend on any theory of Forms. From inside the cave, the shadows are clear and the truth is a painful blur. So the vividness of an experience is no measure of its reality. Sight is good evidence, in other words, and it still has to answer to understanding.
paras.zh: 現在很少有哲學家接受柏拉圖的理型。他自己的學生亞里斯多德就論證過，事物的形式存在於事物之中，在另一個分離的領域裡是找不到的。可是洞穴比它原本要說明的理論活得更久，因為它描述的處境不斷重現。人確實會把事物的影像誤認為事物。任何人對更大的世界所相信的事，有許多是在螢幕上看到的，而安排這些影像的人，始終躲在牆後、不在視線之內。而且這個故事提出了一個關於方法的論點，這個論點並不依賴任何理型論。從洞穴裡面看，影子是清楚的，真相是一片刺痛的模糊。所以一個經驗有多鮮明，並不能衡量它有多真實。換句話說，看見是好的證據，但它仍然得向理解負責。

lab.title_en: Try it: walk through the cave
lab.title_zh: 親手做一次：走一趟洞穴
lab.lead_en: A 3D model built from Plato’s description. The shadows on the wall are real: they are cast by the fire, through the figures carried along the low wall. Start with the whole cave, then follow the five stages of the story. Drag to look around at any point.
lab.lead_zh: 照柏拉圖的描述搭出來的 3D 模型。牆上的影子是真的：由那堆火透過矮牆上被搬運的造像投射出來。先看整個洞穴，再跟著故事的五個階段走。任何時候都可以拖曳畫面環顧四周。

text.en: A cutaway view. Follow the light from right to left: the fire, the figures carried above the low wall, the prisoners facing away, and the back wall where the shadows fall. The way out is the long slope on the right.
text.zh: 剖面全景。順著光從右往左看：火、矮牆上方被搬運的造像、背對著的囚徒，以及影子落下的洞底牆面。出路是右邊那條長長的斜坡。

line.en: Plato matches the journey to four states of mind, the “divided line” of Book VI: imagination, belief, reasoning, and understanding.
line.zh: 柏拉圖把這趟旅程對應到四種心靈狀態，也就是第六卷的「線喻」：想像、信念、推理、理解。

text.en: This is all a prisoner ever sees. The shapes cross the wall in a regular order, and a clever prisoner learns to predict them. Nothing here suggests that they are shadows of anything.
text.zh: 囚徒一輩子看到的就只有這些。形影以固定的次序掠過牆面，聰明的囚徒學會預測它們。這裡沒有任何東西暗示：它們是別的東西的影子。

line.en: Imagination (eikasia): taking images for the things themselves.
line.zh: 想像（eikasia）：把影像當成事物本身。

text.en: Released and made to turn, he sees the wall, the figures, and the fire. The glare hurts, and the real figures look less clear to him than their shadows did. He wants to turn back.
text.zh: 被鬆開、被迫轉身之後，他看見了矮牆、造像與火。強光刺痛他；在他看來，真正的造像還不如它們的影子清楚。他想轉回去。

line.en: Belief (pistis): seeing the objects, with no understanding yet of what they are copies of.
line.zh: 信念（pistis）：看見了物體，但還不明白它們是什麼的仿製品。

text.en: He is dragged up “a steep and rugged ascent.” Plato’s verbs are verbs of force. Nobody leaves the cave by choice, and at this point the light ahead is only painful.
text.zh: 他被人拖上「陡峭崎嶇的上坡」。柏拉圖用的全是強制性的動詞。沒有人是自願離開洞穴的；在這個階段，前方的光只是令人疼痛。

line.en: Reasoning (dianoia): thinking that still leans on images, as geometry leans on diagrams.
line.zh: 推理（dianoia）：仍然倚靠影像的思考，就像幾何學倚靠圖形。

text.en: Outside, he looks first at shadows, then at reflections in the water, then at the things themselves, and at last at the sun. He understands that it is the source of everything he has seen, including the fire below.
text.zh: 到了外面，他先看影子，再看水中的倒影，再看事物本身，最後才看太陽。他明白了：它是他所見一切的來源，連下面那堆火也包括在內。

line.en: Understanding (noēsis): grasping the Forms, and finally the Good.
line.zh: 理解（noēsis）：掌握理型，最後掌握「善」。

text.en: He goes back down. Now he is the one who cannot see, and the prisoners conclude that the journey has ruined him. If he tries to free them, they will kill him if they can.
text.zh: 他回到下面。現在看不見的人換成他了；囚徒們斷定，這趟旅程把他毀了。如果他試著解開他們，他們只要辦得到，就會殺了他。

line.en: Plato’s readers would think of Socrates. In the Republic the return is also a duty: those who have seen the Good must go back and govern.
line.zh: 柏拉圖的讀者會想到蘇格拉底。在《理想國》裡，回來同時是責任：見過「善」的人必須回去治理城邦。

argument.lead_en: The cave is an image and proves nothing by itself. Behind it stands an argument about knowledge, which Plato gives in several dialogues. Click a step to see what can be said against it.
argument.lead_zh: 洞穴是一個意象，本身什麼也沒證明。在它背後有一個關於知識的論證，柏拉圖在好幾部對話錄裡都提出過。點任何一步，看看別人可以怎麼反對它。

steps.en: Knowledge is stable. What is known cannot turn out false tomorrow, so the objects of knowledge must be unchanging.
steps.zh: 知識是穩定的。被知道的事不會明天就變成假的，所以知識的對象必定是不變的。
steps.ob_en: This is the step most often attacked. It slides from a fact about knowing to a claim about what is known. I can know, permanently and truly, that Socrates was sitting at noon, though Socrates has long since stood up. Stable truths do not require unchanging things.
steps.ob_zh: 這是最常被攻擊的一步。它從一個關於「知道」的事實，滑到一個關於「被知道的東西」的主張。我可以永久而且正確地知道「蘇格拉底在中午時坐著」，儘管蘇格拉底早就站起來了。穩定的真理並不需要不變的事物。

steps.en: Everything we perceive is changing, and is what it is only in some respect: equal from here and unequal from there.
steps.zh: 我們感知到的一切都在變，而且只在某個方面是它所是的那樣：從這裡看相等，從那裡看不等。
steps.ob_en: Largely accepted as a description of perceptible things, though Aristotle held that their natures are stable enough to be studied.
steps.ob_zh: 當作對可感事物的描述，這大致被接受；不過亞里斯多德認為，可感事物的本性已經夠穩定，足以成為研究的對象。

steps.en: So perceptible things cannot be objects of knowledge. About them we have only opinion.
steps.zh: 所以可感事物不能是知識的對象。對它們，我們只有意見。
steps.ob_en: If this were right there could be no natural science. The empiricist tradition from Aristotle to Locke takes the success of observation as a refutation.
steps.ob_zh: 如果這是對的，就不可能有自然科學。從亞里斯多德到洛克的經驗論傳統，把觀察的成功當作對這一步的反駁。

steps.en: Yet we do have knowledge, for instance of what equality is and of the properties of the triangle.
steps.zh: 然而我們確實有知識，例如知道相等是什麼、知道三角形的性質。
steps.ob_en: The best evidence for the premise is mathematics. No drawn triangle has angles that sum exactly to two right angles, and yet we know that the triangle’s do. Critics reply that mathematical knowledge may concern our concepts or our rules, with no need of objects in another world.
steps.ob_zh: 這個前提最好的證據是數學。沒有任何畫出來的三角形，內角和恰好等於兩個直角；可是我們知道「三角形」的內角和是。批評者回答：數學知識也許是關於我們的概念或規則的，不需要另一個世界裡的對象。

steps.en: Therefore there exist unchanging objects that are grasped by thought and not perceived: the Forms.
steps.zh: 所以，存在著不變的對象，它們是由思想掌握而不是被感知的：理型。
steps.ob_en: Plato raised the hardest objection himself. If large things are large by sharing in the Form of Largeness, and the Form is itself large, then a further Form is needed to explain what the Form and the things have in common, and so on forever (Parmenides 132a–b). Aristotle named this the Third Man.
steps.ob_zh: 最難的反駁是柏拉圖自己提出來的。如果大的東西之所以大，是因為分有「大的理型」，而這個理型本身也是大的，那就需要再一個理型來解釋理型與那些東西的共同之處；如此下去，沒有盡頭（《巴門尼德篇》132a–b）。亞里斯多德把它命名為「第三人」論證。

source.lead_en: The allegory takes up about four pages at the start of Book VII. It follows directly on two other images, the Sun and the Divided Line, and is meant to be read together with them.
source.lead_zh: 這個寓言在第七卷開頭，大約佔四頁。它緊接在另外兩個意象「日喻」與「線喻」之後，本來就是要跟它們一起讀的。

passages.en: To them, I said, the truth would be literally nothing but the shadows of the images.
passages.zh: 我說，對他們來說，真實簡直就只是那些造像的影子。
passages.note_en: Look closely at the phrase “the shadows of the images.” The prisoners are two steps from reality. What casts the shadows is itself an image, a statue or a carved animal, and the original of that is outside the cave. Plato has built into the picture his view that an ordinary physical object is already a copy.
passages.note_zh: 仔細看「造像的影子」這個詞組。囚徒離實在隔了兩層。投下影子的東西本身就是影像——一尊人像或一隻雕出來的動物——而它的原型在洞穴之外。柏拉圖把他的一個看法做進了這幅圖裡：平常的物體，本身已經是仿製品。

passages.en: …the power and capacity of learning exists in the soul already; and that just as the eye was unable to turn from darkness to light without the whole body, so too the instrument of knowledge can only by the movement of the whole soul be turned from the world of becoming into that of being…
passages.zh: ……學習的能力本來就在靈魂之中；而且，正如眼睛不連著整個身體就無法從黑暗轉向光明，認識的工具也只有藉著整個靈魂的運動，才能從生成變化的世界轉向存有的世界……
passages.note_en: The key phrase is “the whole soul.” The intellect cannot be turned by itself, any more than the eye can. A person’s desires and habits have to turn with it. The Greek word for this turning, periagōgē, was later translated into Latin as conversio, and it is the origin of our word “conversion.”
passages.note_zh: 關鍵的詞組是「整個靈魂」。理智沒辦法單獨被轉過去，就像眼睛沒辦法單獨轉一樣；一個人的欲望與習慣必須跟著一起轉。希臘文稱這個轉向為 periagōgē，後來譯成拉丁文 conversio，就是英文 conversion（皈依、轉化）一詞的來源。

items.o_en: The allegory slanders the only world we have. By placing reality somewhere else, it teaches contempt for the body, the senses, and ordinary life.
items.o_zh: 這個寓言誣衊了我們僅有的這個世界。它把實在放到別處，等於教人輕視身體、感官與平常的生活。
items.r_en: Nietzsche made this charge with great force and traced a long history of world-denial back to Plato. A defender can answer that the prisoner who has seen the sun understands the cave better than before, and goes back to it. Still, the charge has weight. Plato’s image does rank the visible world below another, and much later thought, religious and secular, inherited that ranking.
items.r_zh: 尼采極有力地提出了這項指控，並且把一段漫長的「否定世界」的歷史追溯到柏拉圖。辯護的人可以回答：見過太陽的囚徒對洞穴的了解比從前更深，而且他回去了。不過這項指控是有分量的。柏拉圖的意象確實把可見的世界排在另一個世界之下，而後來許多思想，宗教的與世俗的，都繼承了這個排序。

items.o_en: Anyone can claim to have seen the sun. The story gives the prisoners no way of telling a philosopher from a fraud, and it is used to justify rule by those who say they know best.
items.o_zh: 誰都可以自稱見過太陽。這個故事沒有給囚徒任何辦法去分辨哲學家與騙子，而它被用來替「自稱最懂的人來統治」辯護。
items.r_en: Karl Popper pressed this objection in 1945, writing in exile from a Europe ruled by people who were certain they knew. Plato’s answer is the fifteen-year program of mathematics and argument that follows in Book VII: the claim to have seen is to be tested by one’s ability to give an account and to defend it under questioning. That is a real safeguard inside philosophy. As a rule for deciding who should hold power, most readers today think it is not nearly enough.
items.r_zh: 波普在 1945 年力陳這個反駁；他寫作時流亡在外，而當時統治歐洲的，正是一群確信自己什麼都知道的人。柏拉圖的回答，是第七卷接下來那套十五年的數學與論辯訓練：一個人自稱見過，要用他能不能給出說明、並且在詰問之下守得住來檢驗。在哲學內部，這是一道真正的防線。但當作決定誰該掌權的規則，今天多數讀者認為它遠遠不夠。

items.o_en: A picture is not an argument. The cave assumes what it needs to show, that there is an “outside” at all.
items.o_zh: 圖像不是論證。洞穴預設了它需要證明的事：到底有沒有一個「外面」。
items.r_en: This is correct, and Plato knew it: Socrates introduces the story with the words “let me show in a figure.” The argument for an outside is the one set out above, and it must be judged on its merits. What the image adds is a warning about that judgment. If Plato is right, the truth will look less convincing than the illusion to anyone who is still chained, so a feeling of obviousness cannot settle the matter either way.
items.r_zh: 這是對的，而且柏拉圖自己知道：蘇格拉底是用「讓我用一個比喻來說明」這句話引出故事的。支持「有一個外面」的論證是上面攤開的那一個，它必須就它本身的優劣來評判。這個意象增添的，是對這個評判的一項警告。如果柏拉圖是對的，那麼對任何仍被鍊著的人來說，真相看起來會比幻象更沒有說服力；所以「顯然如此」的感覺，不管往哪一邊，都無法定奪這件事。

said.claim: “We can easily forgive a child who is afraid of the dark; the real tragedy of life is when men are afraid of the light.”
said.claim_zh: 「孩子怕黑，我們很容易原諒；人生真正的悲劇，是成人怕光。」
said.en: This line is attributed to Plato all over the internet and appears in none of his works. It reads like a modern summary of the cave. Plato’s point is in fact harsher than the quotation: the prisoners are not afraid of the light. They have no idea that there is any.
said.zh: 這句話在網路上到處被歸給柏拉圖，卻不見於他的任何著作。它讀起來像是現代人對洞穴寓言的摘要。柏拉圖的重點其實比這句話更嚴厲：囚徒並不是怕光，他們根本不知道有光。

terms.d_en: A story in which the persons and events stand for something else.
terms.d_zh: 故事裡的人物與事件另有所指的敘事。

terms.d_en: In Plato, the unchanging reality (justice itself, the triangle itself) of which particular things are imperfect copies.
terms.d_zh: 在柏拉圖，指不變的實在（正義本身、三角形本身），個別事物是它不完美的仿製品。

terms.d_en: The distinction between how things seem and how they are.
terms.d_zh: 事物看起來的樣子，與事物實際的樣子，兩者的區分。

terms.d_en: Belief about changing, perceptible things, contrasted with knowledge.
terms.d_zh: 關於變動的、可感事物的信念，與知識相對。

terms.d_en: Secure understanding of what cannot be otherwise; the root of “epistemology.”
terms.d_zh: 對「不可能是別樣」的事物的確切理解；epistemology（知識論）的字根。

terms.d_en: What can be grasped by thought and not by the senses.
terms.d_zh: 能由思想掌握、而不能由感官掌握的東西。

terms.d_en: Plato’s word for education: the turning of the whole soul toward what is real.
terms.d_zh: 柏拉圖對教育的稱呼：整個靈魂轉向真實。

terms.d_en: The objection that the theory of Forms leads to an infinite regress of Forms.
terms.d_zh: 指理型論會導致理型無窮後退的那個反駁。

vocab.eg: As a rule of thumb, “seeing is believing” is a good one.
vocab.eg_zh: 當作經驗法則，「眼見為憑」是不錯的。

vocab.eg: The movement hurts, and the fire dazzles him.
vocab.eg_zh: 這個動作讓他疼痛，火光讓他目眩。

vocab.eg: His eyes adjust by stages.
vocab.eg_zh: 他的眼睛是一階一階適應的。

vocab.eg: The world outside stands for what can be grasped only by thinking.
vocab.eg_zh: 洞外的世界代表只有靠思考才能掌握的東西。

vocab.eg: Justice itself, as opposed to this or that just act.
vocab.eg_zh: 正義本身，而不是這個或那個正義的行為。

vocab.eg: We know equality well enough to see that the sticks fall short.
vocab.eg_zh: 我們對相等知道得夠清楚，才看得出那些棍子有所不足。

vocab.eg: The student may well resent the person who causes the turning.
vocab.eg_zh: 學生很可能怨恨促成這次轉身的人。

vocab.eg: The cave has outlived the theory it was built to illustrate.
vocab.eg_zh: 洞穴比它原本要說明的理論活得更久。

vocab.eg: The situation it describes keeps recurring.
vocab.eg_zh: 它描述的處境不斷重現。

vocab.eg: Sight is good evidence, and it still has to answer to understanding.
vocab.eg_zh: 看見是好的證據，但它仍然得向理解負責。

quiz.q: What are the prisoners actually looking at?
options: Shadows of carried figures, cast on the wall by a fire behind them.
The people who walk past the cave mouth.
Reflections of the sun in a pool.
Paintings on the wall of the cave.

quiz.q: In Socrates’ own explanation, what does the cave stand for?
options: The world revealed by the senses.
The afterlife.
The city of Athens only.
The human body.

quiz.q: Why does Plato think knowledge requires Forms?
options: Perceptible things change, and he holds that the objects of knowledge must be stable.
The senses never give any information.
The gods have told us so.
Words have no meaning without pictures.

quiz.q: What view of education does Socrates draw from the cave?
options: It is a turning of the whole soul, and no knowledge is put in from outside.
It is the transfer of facts from teacher to student.
It should be limited to mathematics.
It is impossible.

quiz.q: What happens when the freed prisoner returns?
options: He cannot see in the dark, and the others conclude that the journey ruined him.
He is welcomed and made king.
He finds the cave empty.
He forgets everything he saw.

write.en: Describe a time when you learned that something you had taken for the thing itself was only an image of it. What was the “turning” like, and did you welcome it?
write.zh: 描述一次你發現：某個你一直當成「事物本身」的東西，其實只是它的影像。那次「轉身」是什麼感覺？你歡迎它嗎？

write.en: Socrates says a teacher does not put knowledge into the student. Is he right? Answer in about 150 words, using one example from your own teaching or learning.
write.zh: 蘇格拉底說，老師並不是把知識放進學生裡面。他說得對嗎？用大約 150 個英文字回答，並舉一個你自己教學或學習的例子。

write.en: Who are the carriers behind the wall today? Choose one example and say what would count as “turning around” in that case.
write.zh: 今天躲在矮牆後面搬運造像的人是誰？選一個例子，並說明在那個情況裡，怎樣才算「轉過身去」。

paras.en: A Buddhist reader recognizes a great deal in the cave. There is a condition of bondage that the bound do not notice, which the tradition calls avidyā, ignorance. There is a path of gradual seeing. And there is the return. The one who has seen and goes back among the prisoners out of pity, expecting to be mocked, is very close to the Mahāyāna ideal of the bodhisattva, who declines to rest in his own liberation while others remain bound. The Lotus Sūtra tells a comparable story of a father who coaxes his children out of a burning house in which they are happily playing.
paras.zh: 佛教的讀者在洞穴裡認得出許多東西。有一種被束縛而不自知的狀態，傳統稱之為無明（avidyā）。有一條逐步看見的道路。還有「回來」。那個見過之後、出於憐憫回到囚徒當中、而且預料會被嘲笑的人，非常接近大乘的菩薩理想：別人還被綁著，他就不肯安住在自己的解脫裡。《法華經》講了一個可以相比的故事：父親把正玩得開心的孩子們，從著火的房子裡哄出來。

paras.en: On what is seen outside, the two part completely. Plato’s freed prisoner finds permanent, self-standing essences, and they are more real than anything in the cave. The Madhyamaka philosophers taught two truths, conventional and ultimate, which sounds like the same division. But their ultimate truth is not a second world of better objects. It is the emptiness of the things of this world: the fact that nothing, anywhere, has the kind of independent, unchanging nature that a Platonic Form is supposed to have. For Nāgārjuna, the belief in fixed essences is the chain. On his view the prisoner turns around and finds no sun. What he comes to see is that even the fire and the wall arise in dependence on conditions, and this is the insight that frees him (Dharma and the West, D10).
paras.zh: 至於在外面看見了什麼，兩者徹底分道揚鑣。柏拉圖那位被釋放的囚徒找到的是恆常、自立的本質，而且它們比洞裡的任何東西都更真實。中觀學派的哲學家講二諦，世俗諦與勝義諦，聽起來像是同一種劃分。但他們的勝義諦不是「另一個擺著更好的東西的世界」。它是這個世界的事物之「空」：不管在哪裡，沒有任何東西具有柏拉圖的理型被認為具有的那種獨立、不變的本性。對龍樹來說，相信有固定的本質，那才是鎖鍊。照他的看法，囚徒轉過身去，並沒有找到太陽。他看見的是：連那堆火、那道牆，也都是依條件而生起的；讓他自由的，正是這個洞見（佛法與西方哲學 D10）。

further.t: Plato, Republic, Books VI–VII, translated by Benjamin Jowett
further.n_en: Read the Sun (507b–509c), the Line (509d–511e), and the Cave (514a–521b) together.

further.t: Plato, Parmenides 130a–135c
further.n_en: Plato’s own objections to the Forms, including the Third Man.
further.n_zh: 柏拉圖自己對理型論的反駁，包括第三人論證。

further.t: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Plato’s Middle Period Metaphysics and Epistemology”
Iris Murdoch, The Sovereignty of Good (1970)
further.n_en: A modern philosopher and novelist takes the cave seriously as moral psychology.
further.n_zh: 一位現代哲學家兼小說家，把洞穴當成道德心理學認真對待。

further.t: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “The Theory of Two Truths in India”

lessons.title: Are We Born Knowing Anything?
lessons.title_zh: 我們生下來就知道什麼嗎？
lessons.blurb_en: Plato’s slave boy, Locke’s white paper, Mencius’s child, and the long quarrel between reason and experience over where knowledge comes from.
lessons.blurb_zh: 柏拉圖筆下的少年、洛克的白紙、孟子的孩提之童，以及理性與經驗之間那場漫長的爭論：知識從哪裡來？
lessons.big_en: Experience supplies the content of what we know, and yet a mind with nothing in it could not learn from experience at all. The live question is how much structure a mind must bring.
lessons.big_zh: 我們所知的內容由經驗供應；可是一個裡面什麼都沒有的心靈，根本無法從經驗學到任何東西。真正的問題是：心靈必須自備多少結構？

paras.en: A newborn can do very little, and within five years the same child speaks a language, recognizes faces, counts, and has firm opinions about what is fair. Where did all of that come from? There seem to be only two possible sources. It was put in from outside, by the senses and by teaching, or it was in some form there already. The first answer is called empiricism and the second rationalism or, in its modern form, nativism. The dispute between them is the oldest in the theory of knowledge, and it is unusual among philosophical disputes because experiments now bear on it.
paras.zh: 新生兒能做的事非常少；不出五年，同一個孩子會說一種語言、認得出人臉、會數數，而且對什麼叫公平有堅定的意見。這一切是從哪裡來的？可能的來源似乎只有兩個：由感官與教導從外面放進去的；或者它以某種形式本來就在那裡。第一個答案叫作經驗主義，第二個叫理性主義，它的現代版本稱為先天論。這兩者的爭論是知識論裡最古老的一場；而它在哲學爭論中很特別，因為現在有實驗可以介入。

paras.en: The first great argument for inborn knowledge is a demonstration. In Plato’s Meno, Socrates calls over a household slave, a boy who has never been taught geometry, draws a square in the sand, and asks him how long the side of a square twice as large would be. The boy answers confidently and wrongly, twice. Socrates then draws a few more lines and goes on asking questions, and the boy arrives at the correct answer, which is a hard one. Socrates insists that he told the boy nothing. “Without any one teaching him he will recover his knowledge for himself, if he is only asked questions.”
paras.zh: 支持「天生知識」的第一個重要論證，是一場示範。在柏拉圖的《美諾篇》裡，蘇格拉底叫來一個家奴，一個從沒學過幾何的少年；他在沙地上畫了一個正方形，問少年：面積兩倍大的正方形，邊長是多少？少年很有把握地答錯了，而且錯了兩次。蘇格拉底接著又畫了幾條線，繼續提問；少年得出了正確答案，而那是個不容易的答案。蘇格拉底堅持，他什麼也沒有告訴少年。「沒有任何人教他，只要有人問他問題，他就會自己把知識找回來。」

paras.en: Plato’s explanation is that the soul existed before birth and learned everything then, so that “all enquiry and all learning is but recollection.” Few people have accepted the explanation. The demonstration is harder to dismiss. The boy did not learn the theorem by measuring squares, and once he sees it he sees that it must be so. Truths of that kind, known independently of experience, are called a priori, and they are the rationalist’s best evidence.
paras.zh: 柏拉圖的解釋是：靈魂在出生之前就存在，並且在那時學會了一切，所以「一切探究、一切學習，都不過是回憶」。很少有人接受這個解釋。但那場示範比較難打發。少年並不是靠測量正方形學到這條定理的；而且他一旦看出來，就看出它「非如此不可」。這一類不依賴經驗而被知道的真理，稱為先驗的（a priori），是理性主義者最好的證據。

paras.en: The classic statement of the other side is John Locke’s, in An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690). “Let us then suppose the mind to be, as we say, white paper, void of all characters, without any ideas:—How comes it to be furnished?” His answer is one word: “from EXPERIENCE.” Experience has two channels. Sensation gives us ideas of yellow, hot, hard, and sweet. Reflection, the mind’s notice of its own operations, gives us ideas of thinking, doubting, and willing. Every other idea, however abstract, is built by combining and comparing these.
paras.zh: 另一邊的經典陳述出自洛克的《人類理解論》（1690）。「那麼讓我們假設，心靈就像我們所說的那樣，是一張白紙，上面沒有任何記號，沒有任何觀念：它是怎麼被填滿的？」他的回答只有一個詞：「來自經驗。」經驗有兩個管道。感覺給我們黃、熱、硬、甜的觀念。反省，也就是心靈對自己運作的察覺，給我們思考、懷疑、意願的觀念。其他一切觀念，不管多抽象，都是把這些拿來組合、比較而造出來的。

paras.en: Locke had an argument as well as a picture. If any principles were stamped on the mind at birth, he said, everyone would be aware of them, and children plainly are not aware of the laws of logic. He also had a motive. Claims of innate truth had been used to put favored doctrines beyond question, and a mind that begins blank has to be given reasons.
paras.zh: 洛克除了有一幅圖像，也有論證。他說，如果有任何原則在出生時就印在心靈上，那麼每個人都會察覺到它們；而小孩顯然並沒有察覺到邏輯定律。他也有動機。「天生真理」的說法，曾經被用來讓受偏愛的教條不容質疑；而一個從空白開始的心靈，別人必須給它理由。

paras.en: Leibniz read Locke’s Essay and wrote a book-length reply. He granted that nothing is in the intellect which was not first in the senses, and added three words: except the intellect itself. Locke had taken “innate” to mean “consciously present from birth,” which is easy to refute. The serious claim is that the mind has built-in tendencies. It is less like blank paper, Leibniz said, than like a block of marble with veins in it. The sculptor’s blows are needed to bring the figure out, and the veins make it easier to carve one figure than another. Experience is the occasion of our knowledge of necessary truths. It cannot be the source of their necessity, since no number of observed cases shows that a thing must be so.
paras.zh: 萊布尼茲讀了洛克的《人類理解論》，寫了一整本書來回應。他承認「凡在理智中的，無不先在感官中」，然後加了幾個字：理智本身除外。洛克把「天生」理解成「從出生起就有意識地在場」，那很容易駁倒。嚴肅的主張是：心靈有內建的傾向。萊布尼茲說，與其說它像白紙，不如說它像一塊帶有紋路的大理石。要把雕像顯現出來，需要雕刻家的敲擊；而紋路使得雕出某個形象比雕出另一個容易。經驗是我們認識必然真理的機緣；它不可能是那些真理之必然性的來源，因為觀察到再多個案，也無法顯示一件事「非如此不可」。

essay.h_en: The child who loves his parents

paras.en: In China the same question was asked about morality. Mencius, in the fourth century BCE, held that the beginnings of goodness are part of our original equipment. “What people are able to do without having learned it is their innate ability; what they know without having to reflect is their innate knowledge (良知). There are no young children who do not know to love their parents.” Humaneness and rightness, he says elsewhere, “are not welded onto us from outside; we have them from the start.” He did not think that this made anyone good automatically. The beginnings are sprouts, and a sprout that is neglected dies. His opponent Xunzi argued that goodness is the product of deliberate effort and ritual training imposed on a nature that would otherwise run to conflict. Leibniz’s marble and Locke’s paper had been set against each other, on moral ground, two thousand years before either man was born.
paras.zh: 在中國，同一個問題是針對道德問的。西元前四世紀的孟子主張，善的端倪是我們原初配備的一部分。「人之所不學而能者，其良能也；所不慮而知者，其良知也。孩提之童，無不知愛其親者。」他在別處說，仁義禮智「非由外鑠我也，我固有之也」。他並不認為這樣就讓任何人自動成為好人。那些端倪是芽，而芽被忽略就會死。他的對手荀子則論證說，善是刻意努力與禮的訓練的產物，是加在一個本來會走向爭奪的本性之上的。萊布尼茲的大理石與洛克的白紙，早在這兩個人出生的兩千年前，就已經在道德的領域裡對峙過了。

paras.en: A century after Locke, Immanuel Kant proposed terms of peace. “Though all our knowledge begins with experience,” he wrote, “it by no means follows that all arises out of experience.” The senses supply the material. The mind supplies the form in which any material must be arranged in order to be experienced at all: it places things in space and time and connects them as cause and effect. We are not born knowing any facts, on this view. We are born with the framework that makes facts available to us. Whether Kant identified the right framework is disputed. That some framework is needed is now close to common ground.
paras.zh: 洛克之後一個世紀，康德提出了議和的條件。他寫道：「雖然我們的一切知識都始於經驗，卻絕不能因此說它全都出於經驗。」感官供應材料。心靈供應的是形式：任何材料要成為經驗，都必須被安排進這個形式裡；心靈把事物放在空間與時間之中，並且把它們連結成因與果。照這個看法，我們並不是生來就知道任何事實；我們生來就帶著讓事實得以向我們呈現的那個框架。康德認定的框架對不對，還有爭議。但「需要某種框架」，現在已經接近共識。

paras.en: Three lines of research have changed the debate.
